title: Effect of ambient temperature on marathon pacing is dependent on runner ability
authors: Ely MR, Martin DE, Cheuvront SN, Montain SJ
population: Three Japanese women's championship marathons, 62 race-year outcomes: winner and 25th, 50th, 100th place finishers with 5 km splits
findings: Winners ran even pace; lesser-ability runners slowed as the race progressed, particularly after 20-25 km.
Pace differential (last 5 km minus first 5 km) for 100th place was the same in cool (5-10 C) and warm (15.1-21 C): 199 +/- 45 s vs 198 +/- 40 s.
For the 50th place it tended to increase with warmth (115 +/- 16 vs 163 +/- 27 s) but was not significant.
Warmer weather significantly slowed pace (P < 0.05) for the 25th place (90 +/- 25 vs 191 +/- 20 s) and winners (-22 +/- 14 vs 24 +/- 13 s).

Conclusion: warm air slows pace more in faster runners (winner, 25th) than slower ones (50th, 100th); slower runners' larger finishing-time loss comes from a slower velocity from start to finish rather than a greater late deceleration.
limitations: Women's elite to sub-elite only, air temperature 5-21 C, 5 km splits, small groups, one country, air temperature rather than WBGT.
implications: For slower runners, apply the heat penalty as a uniformly slower target pace from the start, not as a planned fade.
For fast runners (roughly top quartile of a field), expect a heat-driven late-race deceleration; use a more conservative first half in warm weather instead of the cool-weather even-pace target.
Keep the within-race pacing adjustment a tunable parameter; evidence stops near 21 C air temperature.

verification.notes: Crossref (MSSE 2008-09, Ely) and PubMed abstract re-fetched; every number matches (the 163 s value appears as '16 3' in the source text). The 25th-place cool/warm values look odd but are as published. Ely 2007 vs Ely 2008 is a difference of outcome (finishing time vs within-race deceleration), not a contradiction.
